Q1. Operating System Selection and Resource Management

Material to Understand

An Operating System (OS) is software that connects users and applications to computer hardware. It manages important resources such as the CPU, RAM, storage, and input/output devices. Different operating systems, such as Windows and Linux, can be selected based on the applications required, ease of use, hardware compatibility, and efficient resource management. CPU scheduling allows multiple applications to share processing time, while memory management allocates RAM to running programs.

Situation

A university needs computers for a student laboratory. Students will use web browsers, programming software, and office applications.

Question

a) Recommend a suitable Operating System for these computers and explain your choice.

b) Explain how your recommended Operating System manages the CPU and memory when students run multiple applications.

Model Answer

a) Operating System Recommendation

I recommend Windows because it supports common applications such as Microsoft Office, web browsers, and programming tools. It also provides a user-friendly interface and supports multitasking.

Linux is another suitable choice, especially when the laboratory mainly uses open-source programming tools.

b) CPU and Memory Management

  • CPU Management: The Operating System schedules processes and shares CPU time among running applications.
  • Memory Management: The Operating System allocates RAM to applications and manages their memory usage so multiple programs can run efficiently.

Q2. Operating System Services and Resource Management

Material to Understand

Applications cannot directly perform every hardware operation. They request services from the Operating System through system calls. For example, when an application saves a document, it requests file operations from the OS. The kernel processes these requests, the memory manager manages data in RAM, and the file system organizes and stores files on permanent storage devices such as SSDs. These services allow applications to work safely while sharing computer resources.

Situation

A student opens Microsoft Word, writes a document, and saves it while other applications are running.

Question

a) Explain how Microsoft Word requests the Operating System to save the document using a system call.

b) Explain how the Operating System manages memory and storage during this operation.

Model Answer

a) System Call

A system call is a request from an application to the Operating System for a service.

When the student clicks Save:

  1. Microsoft Word requests a file-saving service through system calls.
  2. The Operating System handles the request and writes the document data to storage.

b) Memory and Storage Management

  • Memory: The Operating System manages the RAM used by Microsoft Word and other running applications.
  • Storage: The Operating System uses the file system to save the document on an SSD or hard disk.

Q3. Processes and Multiprogramming

Material to Understand

A process is a program currently being executed. During execution, a process may move between five main states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, and Terminated. The Operating System manages these states and decides which process receives CPU time. Multiprogramming allows multiple processes to remain in memory so that when one process waits for an event, another ready process can use the CPU. This improves CPU utilization and allows several applications to make progress.

Situation

A student opens Calculator, a web browser, and a music application at the same time.

Question

a) Define a process and explain the five main process states using one of these applications as an example.

b) Explain how the Operating System uses multiprogramming to manage these applications and share CPU time.

Model Answer

a) Process and Five States

A process is a program that is currently running. Example: Calculator application.

StateExplanation
NewThe Calculator process is being created.
ReadyThe Calculator is waiting for CPU time.
RunningThe CPU executes Calculator instructions.
WaitingThe Calculator waits for an event or input.
TerminatedThe Calculator process has finished.

b) Multiprogramming

Multiprogramming allows multiple programs to remain in memory and share CPU resources.

  1. Calculator, Chrome, and the music application are loaded into memory.
  2. The Operating System schedules their processes and switches CPU execution between them.
  3. When one process waits for an event, another ready process can use the CPU.

This improves CPU utilization and allows multiple applications to run during the same period.

Q4. Threads and Process Synchronization

Material to Understand

A process is a running program with its own resources, while a thread is a smaller unit of execution inside a process. Multiple threads can share the same memory and make progress concurrently. When multiple activities need shared resources, synchronization mechanisms control access to prevent conflicts. A mutex allows only one thread to enter a protected critical section at a time, while a counting semaphore controls access to a limited number of available resources.

Situation

A university computer lab has four computers shared by five students. All five students request access at the same time.

Question

a) Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and describe how multithreading supports concurrent execution.

b) Explain how a counting semaphore initialized to 4 manages access to the computers and what happens to the fifth student.

Model Answer

a) Process, Thread, and Multithreading

  • Process: A running program with its own memory space and resources.
  • Thread: A unit of execution inside a process. Threads within the same process share memory and resources.
  • Multithreading: Allows multiple threads inside one process to make progress concurrently.

Example: A music application can use one thread to play music and another to search for songs.

b) Counting Semaphore

A counting semaphore controls access to a limited number of resources.

  1. The semaphore starts with a value of 4, representing four available computers.
  2. Each student who acquires a computer decreases the semaphore count by 1.
  3. The first four students can use the computers.
  4. The fifth student must wait because no computer is available.
  5. When a student releases a computer, the semaphore count increases, allowing a waiting student to acquire it.

Q5. CPU Scheduling Algorithms

Material to Understand

CPU scheduling determines which ready process receives CPU time. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) executes processes in arrival order. Shortest Job First (SJF) selects the process with the shortest CPU burst when all jobs are available. Round Robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time quantum and moves unfinished processes to the back of the ready queue. A Gantt chart shows the execution order and timing. Waiting time measures how long a process spends waiting for CPU execution, and average waiting time can be used to compare scheduling algorithms.
